stories.title_en: Overhearing the Official's Words, Then Going Out to Swindle

paragraphs.en: In the district there was a widow, the richest of all her neighbors. She had only one son, Gan Shu, just come of age, who kept strictly to the family estate and dared not lend money out. A villager named Lu Wu repeatedly asked him for loans of silver and grain; both times Gan Shu refused, and Lu Wu bore him a grudge. Lu went home and plotted with his wife, née Hu, to falsely accuse Gan Shu of rape. His wife agreed: "All right." He also enlisted his close friend Zhi Jiu as a witness, and they went straight to the circuit inspector's office to lodge the charge. The inspector took up the case himself. First he asked Hu, "Why did Gan Shu come to your house?" Hu said, "His family is rich and he idles all day; he does nothing but debauch other men's wives. Knowing my husband was not at home, he came for no reason and made advances on me; when I refused, he seized me and forced kisses on me. I cursed him and still he would not leave. Only when Zhi Jiu came to invite my husband out to buy goods did Gan Shu finally go." Next he asked Zhi Jiu, "What business did you have at Lu Wu's house?" Zhi Jiu said, "Lu Wu and I both make our living carrying goods for sale. I went to invite him to buy stock, heard a woman inside shouting curses, and saw Gan Shu come out." Then he asked Gan Shu, "Why were you quarreling with the woman?" Gan Shu said, "I never set foot in their house—how could there be a quarrel? Ask Lu Wu's neighbors on either side and you will know." The neighbors all said, "Gan Shu is a widow's son and has never dared misbehave. None of us around here has heard of any affair; this is a story cooked up to frame him." Lu Wu shot back, "His family is worth ten thousand—why couldn't he buy a couple of witnesses?" The neighbors said, "We live right next door and know nothing; this Zhi Jiu lives a whole street away—isn't it plain he was bought to testify?" The inspector said, "Lu Wu is a poor man—how could he buy testimony?" He had the neighbors and Gan Shu each given twenty strokes, and was bent on convicting him of rape. Gan Shu left the court in terror, with no idea how to clear himself.

When the evening session ended, the inspector had the gates sealed. He strolled about the rear hall, thinking in silence, then suddenly said to himself, "A mistake! A mistake!" He paced around several more times, then snapped his sleeves and went in. Now a watchman named Tu Shan was outside, spying on the inspector's every move. Hearing him say "a mistake," Tu Shan guessed it must be about this illicit affair. In the dead of night he climbed out over the wall and knocked at the door of the inn where Gan Shu was lodging. The innkeeper opened up and let him in. Gan Shu was sitting in gloom, out of ideas. Tu Shan said, "About today's case—do you want to work an inside connection?" Gan Shu said, "What connection could clear me? That is exactly what I am desperate for." Tu Shan said, "His Honor happens to have his wife's brother visiting, and within three days the man must be seen off with his parting gifts. This channel works like a charm. If you go through him, there will be a rehearing tomorrow, and you will win bigger still." Gan Shu said, "If that can be done, good. How much silver will it take?" Tu Shan said, "This means reversing a case on his own docket—not like an ordinary favor. It will take a hundred taels." Gan Shu said, "A hundred taels I will pay, so long as the case is reheard tomorrow." Tu Shan said, "The uncle's banquet has not yet broken up; I will go in and speak to him at once." Gan Shu and the innkeeper saw him out. The yamen's main gate was already sealed, so Tu Shan climbed back in over the wall by way of a neighboring house.

The next day, after opening morning court, the magistrate immediately ordered a rehearing of the rape case. Gan Shu was overjoyed, believing the connection had worked. In the afternoon, the magistrate questioned Gan Shu again: "Did Lu Wu ever ask you for a loan?" Gan Shu replied, "He twice asked to borrow silver and grain; I refused both times, so he holds a grudge and fabricated this charge." The magistrate then questioned Hu: "Gan Shu never entered your house—how could there be a rape? Seize her!" Since Lu Wu had spent no silver on bribes, the finger-squeezers were tightened mercilessly. Hu could not bear the pain and confessed: "There was no rape. He refused our loan request, so we made up the charge." Lu Wu and Zhi Jiu were each beaten thirty strokes, and Gan Shu was cleared and released. Tu Shan immediately followed him out to demand payment. Gan Shu said, "I will pay gladly." Tu Shan then asked for a personal thank-you gift, and Gan Shu gave him another ten taels. Tu Shan carried the silver into the office, deposited it into the official's account, came back out to beg for an additional token of gratitude, and received another ten taels. At the time, Gan Shu credited everything to the power of his uncle's influence—how could he know it stemmed from the magistrate's sudden change of heart, and that every tael had been swindled away by Tu Shan?

Note: Yamen underlings all feed and clothe their households by swindling—how could their tricks ever be numbered? Every affair is a swindle, every day a swindle, every man a swindler. Use up every bamboo on the southern hills and you still could not write them all down; bring Bao Zheng back to life and even he could not see through them. I have never been one to enter a court of law, and of the abuses within I have heard little; this one I happened to witness with my own eyes, so I record these malpractices as they are. Yet though every man in the yamen is a knave and every business a nest of swindles, I need only pay my public dues early and endure a hundred wrongs rather than go to law—then what can greedy clerks and bullying runners do to me? Hence the saying: a snare may be cunning—the wise course is not to step in it; poison may be deadly—the wise course is not to drink it; yamen men may be cheats—the wise course is not to enter their gates. Even if some undeserved calamity should strike, there is bound to be a clear-sighted official to right the wrong. Why? Officials are all men who have read the books; the clear-headed are many and the muddled few. The pity is that the underlings around them screen them in dark cloud and fog. So swallow small angers and stay out of the yamen—that is the wise course.

stories.title_en: Deceiving with a Heavy Sentence to Release the Prisoner

paragraphs.en: There was a well-to-do commoner named Yuan Zhi, comfortably off and careful in his conduct, from a family decent for generations. By chance he fell out with a powerful man of the district. That man had long been friendly with Judge Ye, so he went hunting for flaws and manufactured more than a dozen charges of Yuan Zhi's "crimes." Judge Ye forwarded them for investigation, and the investigating censor approved the case and assigned it to Ye for trial. Ye had Yuan Zhi brought in and told him, "I already know your misdeeds in full; the punishment is fixed by statute. But your family is rich, so hear this: you are not to beg any inside connections. If there is any back-door pull, your punishment will be increased, not reduced. Take him to jail for now; once the alleged victims have been brought in, the case will be heard and sentence passed." Judge Ye had always been honest and upright and never accepted private intercession. Now that Yuan Zhi had been warned to his face, he dared even less to scheme or stir, and only waited in dread for his sentence.

Now it happened that a close relative, the retired official Yi, had long been on good terms with Yuan Zhi. Knowing the case was an enemy's frame-up, he quietly pleaded Yuan Zhi's cause to the prefect and asked him to put in a word with Judge Ye for a release. The prefect found an opening and spoke gently on his behalf. Judge Ye was enraged. He went back, had Yuan Zhi fetched, and berated him: "I told you not to send in any private word—and you went and got His Honor the prefect to speak for you! A vicious schemer like you—I will certainly sentence you to garrison exile!" Yuan Zhi had no idea where this had come from. He kowtowed: "Your Honor has never accepted back-door appeals—the whole prefecture knows it. And you instructed me to my face; how would I dare beg the prefect? I truly do not know how this arose." Judge Ye said, "Back to jail. It will be a military sentence for certain." Yuan Zhi came out and made inquiries; only then did he learn that the matter had come from the retired official Yi, who had spoken for his release on his own initiative, never letting Yuan Zhi know. Yuan Zhi could think of no way out. He sought out Ling, the scribe who had the judge's ear, and said in secret, "If you can get my military exile reduced to penal servitude, I will thank you with a rich gift." Scribe Ling said, "Put up a hundred taels and I will work it out for you." Yuan Zhi agreed, and sealed up the silver.

Judge Ye did in fact call in Scribe Ling to draft the sentence: "Find a law on military exile and propose it." Ling deliberately proposed strangulation. Judge Ye ordered the draft changed—only military exile would do. A day later Ling again proposed strangulation: "On the investigation list, the heaviest count is scheming to kill his own younger brother, which fits the strangulation statute exactly. The remaining counts, this one and that one, are only servitude offenses; none of them fits a military exile law." Judge Ye thought it over: "Even on a complaint with a named accuser I would not lightly send a man to the cord—still less on a warrantless investigation like this." He said, "Lucky for him. Just propose servitude." In the end the sentence proposed was three years' penal servitude. Yuan Zhi gladly paid the redemption money, and Scribe Ling pocketed the hundred-tael bribe at his ease. As for Judge Ye—how was he to know that outside his clerk had taken gold, while inside he was deliberately proposing too heavy a sentence? So it is when yamen underlings deceive their official: even a magistrate with the insight of a god would not catch it.

Note: The good are commended and the wicked arrested for investigation—this is one of the court's great levers for encouraging virtue and warning vice. Nowadays those commended often owe it to clever toadying and string-pulling, and those investigated are sometimes set upon at the instigation of the powerful; the ratio of false to true cases is now roughly equal. Still, we should be glad this avenue of investigation exists: it can give the cunning and obstinate a scare and let honest folk breathe a little easier. The trouble is that the investigated man's fate rises or falls in the examining judge's mind, while his sentence is pitched high or low in the scheming clerk's hand—so few in the end receive the punishment their case truly merits. When those who hold office and wield power meet a grave case with heavy stakes, they must empty their minds, examine every detail, see clearly and decide with firm resolve; only then can they stop one or two of the cheats.

stories.title_en: A Clerk Berates a Convict to Split the Beating

paragraphs.en: It is told that when Bao Xiaosu held office he was clean-handed and clear-sighted, and applied the law without favor: no cheat could talk his way out with clever arguments, no guilty man could escape through powerful friends, and he accepted no private intercession. So people said of him, "Where no back-door appeal can reach, there stands old Bao, dread as King Yama of the underworld."

It happened that a rich man's son was truly guilty of an illicit affair. Knowing he could not escape Lord Bao's piercing insight, he plotted in advance with a veteran clerk: "Lord Bao is sharp and sees through cases like a god. My offense is real, and direct witnesses confirm it—there is no escaping conviction. A heavy fine I could still pay; it is the painful beating I cannot bear. If there is any scheme to reduce the strokes, I will spare no expense to work it." The veteran clerk said, "Tomorrow, when the beating is about to begin, run up close to the bench and argue stubbornly, begging to be heard. I will bawl you out from the side and take half the strokes for you; perhaps we can cut your share by half. Beyond that, there is no scheme to be had."

The next day, Lord Bao uncovered the truth, flew into a rage, and ordered forty strokes for Fu Zi. Fu Zi rushed up to the bench, clamoring endlessly in self-defense. An old clerk shouted from the side: "Go take your punishment at once! Why all this talk? Do you think your crime will be pardoned?" Lord Bao saw this and bitterly resented the clerk for seizing authority and putting on a show of power. Fearing the man would one day usurp such power to swindle people and cause trouble elsewhere, he first gave the old clerk twenty strokes—and perversely reduced Fu Zi's penalty by twenty—wanting to show that awe did not stem from any clerk. He did not realize he had fallen squarely into their trap. The old clerk then collected a fat bribe, while Lord Bao remained completely unaware.

Note: When clerks work their frauds, it always begins with knowing their own official's temperament and turning it to their use. The veteran clerk knew Lord Bao was strict and clear-sighted and would never let underlings gather power. So he shouted at the prisoner from the side, certain that Lord Bao would beat the clerk and deliberately spare the prisoner—to prove that clerks hold no power and keep outsiders from standing in awe of them. Who would have guessed that, inside a beating that could hardly be reduced, he was splitting the strokes to collect a bribe? And who could possibly detect it? Even Lord Bao was swindled by a clerk—what hope is there for the officials who come after him?
